title: What is a savepoint (`SAVEPOINT sp1` → work → `ROLLBACK TO sp1` to undo only the work after the savepoint while keeping the rest of the transaction), and when do you use it (partial retry within a larger transaction, batch processing where one record fails but you don't want to discard the whole batch)?
shortTitle: SQL Savepoints — Partial Rollback Within a Transaction

s1_definition.profdef: A savepoint is a named marker inside an open transaction. You create it with `SAVEPOINT sp1`, do more work, and if that work fails you issue `ROLLBACK TO sp1` to undo only the changes made after the savepoint while keeping everything before it intact and the transaction still open. It gives you partial rollback granularity, which is useful for retrying one step within a larger transaction or for batch processing where a single bad record should be skipped without discarding the whole batch.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine processing a batch of a hundred salary credits for National Bank of India inside one transaction. Before each credit you drop a bookmark (savepoint). If crediting employee number 57 fails because their account is frozen, you don't tear up the whole batch — you rewind to the bookmark just before 57 (ROLLBACK TO sp57), skip that one, log it, and carry on from 58. The 56 good credits already done stay, and the transaction stays open.
s1_definition.oneliner: A savepoint is a bookmark inside a transaction; ROLLBACK TO it undoes only the work after the bookmark, so one bad step doesn't sink the whole transaction.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A savepoint is a named marker inside an open transaction. You create it with `SAVEPOINT sp1`, do more work, and if that work fails you issue `ROLLBACK TO sp1` to undo only the changes made after the savepoint while keeping everything before it intact and the transaction still open. It gives you partial rollback granularity, which is useful for retrying one step within a larger transaction or for batch processing where a single bad record should be skipped without discarding the whole batch.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine processing a batch of a hundred salary credits for National Bank of India inside one transaction. Before each credit you drop a bookmark (savepoint). If crediting employee number 57 fails because their account is frozen, you don't tear up the whole batch — you rewind to the bookmark just before 57 (ROLLBACK TO sp57), skip that one, log it, and carry on from 58. The 56 good credits already done stay, and the transaction stays open.

**One line to remember:** A savepoint is a bookmark inside a transaction; ROLLBACK TO it undoes only the work after the bookmark, so one bad step doesn't sink the whole transaction.

sections.s2_technical:
Within a transaction you can set any number of savepoints, each with a name. `SAVEPOINT sp1` records the current point. If later work must be undone, `ROLLBACK TO sp1` reverts all changes made after sp1 but does not end the transaction and does not touch anything committed-in-spirit before sp1. You can then continue, commit, or roll back further. `RELEASE SAVEPOINT sp1` discards the savepoint when you no longer need it, freeing resources.

The key distinction from a full ROLLBACK is granularity. A full ROLLBACK throws away the entire transaction. ROLLBACK TO a savepoint is surgical — it rewinds to a point and keeps the rest. Importantly, rolling back to a savepoint invalidates any savepoints created after it, because time has effectively rewound past them.

The classic use is batch processing with per-record isolation. You want the batch to run in one transaction for efficiency, but you do not want one poison record to force the whole batch to roll back. You set a savepoint before each record; on failure you roll back to that savepoint, record the error, and proceed. At the end you commit the good records in one shot.

The second use is partial retry. Inside a long transaction, a single step might fail transiently — for example, a lookup to a flaky resource. You can roll back to a savepoint just before that step and retry it a few times without abandoning the work already done earlier in the transaction.

In JDBC this maps to `Connection.setSavepoint(name)`, which returns a Savepoint object, and `connection.rollback(savepoint)`. In Spring, nested propagation (`Propagation.NESTED`) is implemented using JDBC savepoints under the hood, so an inner method can roll back independently of the outer transaction.

The senior nuance is that savepoints are not free: holding a long transaction with many savepoints keeps locks and undo information around, so for very large batches you often prefer chunking into several shorter transactions instead of one giant transaction with thousands of savepoints.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India runs a nightly salary batch crediting many accounts in one transaction. Occasionally one account is frozen or closed, and crediting it fails. We must not discard the whole batch for one bad record.

Problem 1 — one failure should not sink the batch. Before each credit we set a savepoint. If a credit fails, we roll back to that savepoint, skip the record, and continue. The earlier good credits remain pending in the transaction.

Problem 2 — the good work must still commit atomically. After processing every record, we commit once, so all the good credits land together.

Problem 3 — failures must be recorded. Each skipped record is logged with its reason so operations can follow up.

The code includes a BatchConnection that mimics savepoint semantics, a SalaryBatchService that sets a savepoint per record and rolls back to it on failure, and a demo that processes a batch where one account is frozen.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway)
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id      VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    balance DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    status  VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'   -- ACTIVE or FROZEN
);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES
    ('EMP001',50000.00,'ACTIVE'),
    ('EMP057',0.00,'FROZEN'),
    ('EMP058',30000.00,'ACTIVE');

-- Savepoint pattern in raw SQL:
-- BEGIN;
--   SAVEPOINT sp_emp057;
--   UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 80000 WHERE id='EMP057';  -- fails (frozen)
--   ROLLBACK TO sp_emp057;   -- undo only this credit, keep the rest
-- COMMIT;
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
batch:
  salary-amount: 80000     # flat salary credit per employee for the demo
  commit-at-end: true      # one commit after the whole batch
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a salary batch of Rs.80,000 each for EMP001, EMP057 (frozen), and EMP058, inside one transaction.

Step 1 — Before EMP001, a savepoint sp_EMP001 is set. The credit succeeds; EMP001's pending balance rises from Rs.50,000 to Rs.130,000. The transaction stays open.

Step 2 — Before EMP057, savepoint sp_EMP057 is set. The credit throws because the account is frozen. We ROLLBACK TO sp_EMP057, which rewinds only EMP057's attempted change; EMP001's good credit is untouched. EMP057 is added to the skipped list and logged.

Step 3 — Before EMP058, savepoint sp_EMP058 is set. The credit succeeds; EMP058 rises from Rs.30,000 to Rs.110,000.

Step 4 — After the loop, a single COMMIT persists both good credits atomically. EMP057 stays exactly as it was, and the batch is not lost.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 17:34:00 [INFO] credited EMP001 Rs.80000
2026-10-25 17:34:00 [WARNING] ROLLBACK TO sp_EMP057
2026-10-25 17:34:00 [SEVERE] skipped EMP057: account frozen: EMP057
2026-10-25 17:34:00 [INFO] credited EMP058 Rs.80000
2026-10-25 17:34:00 [INFO] COMMIT
2026-10-25 17:34:00 [INFO] skipped=[EMP057]
2026-10-25 17:34:00 [INFO] EMP001=130000
2026-10-25 17:34:00 [INFO] EMP057=0 (unchanged, frozen)
2026-10-25 17:34:00 [INFO] EMP058=110000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Salary batch [EMP001, EMP057(frozen), EMP058]   (ONE transaction)
    │
    ▼
  SAVEPOINT sp_EMP001 → credit EMP001   pending: EMP001 50k→130k
    │
    ▼
  SAVEPOINT sp_EMP057 → credit EMP057 (frozen)
    │                     └─ ROLLBACK TO sp_EMP057  (undo ONLY EMP057; EMP001 kept)

    │
    ▼
  COMMIT  → EMP001=130k, EMP058=110k persisted; EMP057=0 untouched

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A savepoint is a named marker you set inside an open transaction. You create it with SAVEPOINT followed by a name, do more work, and if that work goes wrong you issue ROLLBACK TO that name, which undoes only the changes made after the savepoint while keeping everything before it and leaving the transaction still open. It is surgical, partial rollback — very different from a full ROLLBACK, which throws away the entire transaction. One subtlety is that rolling back to a savepoint invalidates any savepoints created after it, because you have effectively rewound past them.

The two situations where I reach for savepoints are partial retry and batch processing with per-record isolation. For partial retry, if a single step inside a long transaction fails transiently, I roll back to a savepoint just before that step and retry it without abandoning the earlier work. For batch processing, I want the efficiency of one transaction but I do not want a single poison record to force the whole batch to roll back.

In our National Bank of India nightly salary batch we credit many employee accounts in one transaction, and occasionally one account is frozen so its credit fails. We set a savepoint before each credit; when the frozen account throws, we roll back to its savepoint, which undoes only that one attempted credit, record the account in a skipped list for operations to follow up, and carry on. At the end we commit once, so every good credit lands atomically and the frozen one is simply left untouched. In JDBC this maps to setSavepoint and rollback with the savepoint, and in Spring the NESTED propagation uses savepoints under the hood so an inner method can roll back independently of the outer transaction. The caution I add is that holding a huge transaction with thousands of savepoints keeps locks and undo data alive, so for very large batches I prefer chunking into several shorter transactions. The line I remember is that a savepoint is a bookmark inside a transaction, and rolling back to it undoes only the work after the bookmark, so one bad step never sinks the whole transaction.
